results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing 2026: After Nvidia's 15% Price Hike, What Should Enterprises Do? | Lieke Tech
highlights:
## 1. The Price Hike Is Real: What Happened?

On August 22, 2026, Bloomberg reported that Nvidia has notified its largest customers — including Microsoft, Google, and Oracle — that servers powered by its next-generation AI chips will see price increases of over 15%, with some configurations nearing 17%. The new prices take effect for early 2027 shipments of Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell systems.

Key figures:

- H100 one-year rental climbed from $1.70/GPU/hour (Oct 2025) to $2.35 — a 38% increase
- H200 rental now at $3.50/GPU/hour
- 8x H200 server monthly rental: ~$11,500 USD
- RTX 4090 scalped to ~$7,000 on secondary markets
- On-demand GPU capacity essentially sold out globally; high-end cards backordered into 2028

The primary driver is memory. Per TrendForce, Q1 2026 DRAM contract prices surged 90-95% quarter-over-quarter, with another 58-63% increase expected in Q2. The big three memory makers are shifting capacity to HBM, creating a severe shortage of standard DRAM. Memory now accounts for 62% of the Vera Rubin superchip's bill of materials.

results.title: ISSUE #7: The B300 Trickle
highlights:
### Bobby Clay 

 Published Aug 25, 2026 

 Weekly Cloud Pricing Pulse, week ending August 24, 2026: the floor held, and an established chip is still finding its public price 

 Published August 25, 2026 · Pricing evidence through August 24, 2026 · Ornn Compute Price Index (OCPI) through August 23, 2026, 20:00 UTC. 

 The LinkedIn edition of the AIForge Works Weekly Cloud Pricing Pulse: one read on public GPU cloud pricing across nine providers, every week. 

 The one-line read. The four public floors did not move this week: H100 SXM $3.85, H200 $4.29, B200 $6.69, A100 SXM4 $2.30, the same levels we have shown since mid-July. Two things moved around them. The OCPI transaction index rose under three of the four floors, narrowing every gap on the board. And the B300, a chip that has been shipping since last year, is still finding a public price: only a few clouds list it on-demand, intermittently, and where they do the numbers range from about $7.85 to about $26.15 per GPU-hour. A settled floor, a firming index underneath it, and an established Blackwell GPU whose public price is still a trickle. 

## This week 

- Floors held. All four board floors are unchanged: H100 SXM $3.85 (Nebius), H200 $4.29 (Crusoe), B200 $6.69 (Lambda), A100 SXM4 $2.30 (Crusoe), the same levels we have published since mid-July. Across all nine indexed providers, no comparable public on-demand rate moved more than 1% week over week.
- The index moved under them. The floors held, but the OCPI transaction index did not. Week over week it rose for H100 ($2.64 to $2.87), B200 ($5.93 to $6.64), and A100 SXM4 ($1.02 to $1.07), and fell for H200 ($4.75 to $4.42). With the floors flat, every gap on the board narrowed. B200’s floor is now just $0.05 above the index, the tightest spread on the board.
- The B300 trickle. The B300 is an established Blackwell-generation GPU, in market since last year, with prior history in the AIForge Works catalog. What is still catching up is its public price. Only a handful of clouds list it on-demand, and they do so intermittently: AWS’s eight-GPU p6-b300.48xlarge appeared in Seoul for the first time in our reviewed history this week (Linux and four licensed operating-system variants), while Nebius listings dropped and then returned. We now see publicly listed on-demand B300 rates from three providers, AWS, OCI, and Nebius; CoreWeave shows the SKU but its rate is still contact-sales. The listed rates disagree sharply, from about $7.85 per GPU-hour (Nebius, three regions) to about $26.15 (AWS, Seoul). That is catalog visibility, not orderable capacity, and it is what a chip still finding its public price looks like.

### GPU Floor Board

 Every floor on this board is still a neocloud, and each has held its level since mid-July. 

 What changed this week is underneath: three of the four index values rose toward the floor, so the board’s spreads are the narrowest we have shown. Read the board as a reference gap, not a quote. These are the lowest indexed public catalog rates, which is not the same as orderable, in stock, or inclusive of negotiated terms. 

 A flat floor can look like a market asleep. This week it was the opposite. The four numbers you would take into a renewal did not move, H100 $3.85, H200 $4.29, B200 $6.69, A100 SXM4 $2.30. But the OCPI transaction index rose under three of them, and B200’s floor went from $0.76 above the index a week ago to $0.05 above it now. The catalog floor held; the transactional market moved up to meet it. That is a firming market, not a soft one, and it is the kind of thing a single weekly number would miss if it only reported the floor. 

 The other thing worth watching is not a new chip; it is an existing one still finding a public number. The B300 has been shipping since last year, yet a clean public on-demand price for it is still a trickle: a few clouds, listed intermittently, at rates that run from single digits to the mid-twenties per GPU-hour, dependent on provider, region, and instance. That is not a bargain and a rip-off sitting side by side; it is what price discovery looks like before a market settles. Watching it narrow, week by week, is how you will see a real B300 floor form. And the genuine next generation, NVIDIA’s Rubin line and AMD’s MI400, has not reached a public on-demand price we can track yet, which tells you where the transparency actually is: a generation behind the frontier, and only now filling in. Catalog visibility is not orderability, and none of these are live quotes, but they are where the next negotiation starts. 

### Reading The Pulse numbers

 The public catalog rates AIForge Works presents are on-demand and normalized to a per-GPU-hour basis unless stated otherwise. OCPI is transaction-index context, not a catalog price. Listed or indexed does not mean orderable, and neither is a live quote, an availability guarantee, or a purchase recommendation. Verify current pricing, availability, terms, and fees directly with the provider before acting.

results.title: Rent, reserve or own GPUs: how to choose | SSP
highlights:
#### What the market actually charges

- Renting an H100 SXM on a specialist GPU cloud runs roughly $1.49 to $3.50 per GPU per hour on demand, with H200 starting near $3.72 and B200 between $2.12 and $6.04 depending on tier and commitment. Source: GPU rental market survey, GetDeploying GPU Price Index and provider pricing pages, 2026
- Hyperscalers charge around 86% more than dedicated GPU clouds for the same H100 silicon. Source: Compute Exchange, Best GPU Rental Platforms 2026
- Owned H100 nodes in the current secondary market sit near $240,000 for an 8-GPU node, which is where the rent-versus-own arithmetic starts to bite at sustained utilisation. Source: SSP verified inventory, August 2026

Renting is on-demand cloud: pay by the hour, walk away whenever. Reserving is committed capacity: a defined rate for a defined term on dedicated hardware, usually bare metal in a named facility. Owning is exactly what it sounds like: the nodes are yours, along with everything that comes with them.

results.title: packet.ai vs Verda: GPU Cloud Comparison 2026 | packet.ai
highlights:
B200 from $4.25/hr, RTX 4090 from $0.39/hr. Hourly, no contract.

Verda is the new name for DataCrunch, the Helsinki-based GPU cloud that runs on renewable energy in Finland and Iceland and has quietly built one of the broadest Blackwell rate cards in Europe: B200, B300, GB300, alongside H200, H100, A100, RTX Pro 6000 and L40S. Its distinguishing feature is a published spot tier at 50% of on-demand across the board, plus a serverless container product.

packet.ai reaches similar prices with a different mechanism: Dynamic instances that share a card under scheduler-enforced isolation and are never pre-empted. This comparison lines up Verda's on-demand and spot columns against packet.ai's Dynamic and Dedicated.

...

### What Verda offers

Verda's published on-demand rates as of late August 2026: GB300 $8.62/hr, B300 $7.50/hr, B200 $6.11/hr, H200 SXM $4.00/hr, H100 SXM $3.25/hr, RTX Pro 6000 (96GB) $1.89/hr, A100 SXM 80GB $1.79/hr, A100 40GB $1.29/hr, L40S $1.37/hr, RTX 6000 Ada $1.04/hr, RTX A6000 $0.61/hr. Spot is 50% of on-demand on every card (B200 $3.06, H200 $2.00, RTX Pro 6000 about $0.95). Reserved terms from 1 to 24 months discount 2–25%.

- Per-second billing, no minimum commitment; instances from 1× to 8× on most cards
- Renewable-powered data centres in Finland and Iceland; ISO-certified; strong EU residency story
- Serverless containers priced separately (H100 $3.58/hr, L40S $1.51/hr) with spot at about half
- Confidential-computing variants of B200 and RTX Pro 6000 at a small premium

...

On-demand to on-demand, packet.ai is cheaper on every shared card: RTX Pro 6000 60% less, A100 80GB 50% less, and B200 Dynamic 30% less than Verda's on-demand rate.

- Dynamic: scheduler-enforced multi-tenant, never pre-empted. RTX 6000 Pro at $0.76/hr, below Verda's own spot rate for the same card. A100 80GB at $0.89/hr, 50% under Verda's on-demand. B200 at $4.25/hr, 30% under Verda's on-demand.
- Dedicated: a whole card, single-tenant, 99% SLA, for workloads that need guaranteed exclusivity rather than shared scheduling. RTX 4090 at $0.39/hr, B200 at $7.99/hr.

What Verda has that packet.ai does not: H100, H200 and B300 on the rate card today, a true spot tier for checkpointed training that can beat Dynamic on the largest cards, confidential-computing variants, and Nordic renewable-powered residency. If your workload is Hopper-class and can tolerate interruption, Verda's spot tier is genuinely hard to beat. If you need non-interruptible capacity at a price below anyone's spot rate, packet.ai's Dynamic tier does that on the RTX Pro 6000 specifically.

...

### On-demand versus on-demand

Card for card at list price, packet.ai is lower everywhere the two overlap: RTX Pro 6000 $0.76 against $1.89 (60% less), A100 80GB $0.89 against $1.79 (50% less). On the B200, packet.ai Dynamic at $4.25 is 30% under Verda's $6.11, while packet.ai Dedicated at $7.99 is 31% above it.

Verda has Hopper and B300 on the card today; packet.ai has notify lists. If your workload is H100-shaped, Verda's $3.25/hr H100 SXM is one of the better published prices in Europe.

results.title: Nvidia AI Price Hikes: 15%+ on AI Hardware

Nvidia has informed customers of price increases exceeding 15% on AI-related products, according to a Bloomberg News report. The hikes, which cover data center GPUs and networking equipment, are set to impact enterprises and developers relying on Nvidia's AI stack.

## What's Affected

While the report doesn't specify exact SKUs, the price adjustments target Nvidia's AI-focused hardware line, including accelerators like the H100 and A100, as well as InfiniBand networking gear. The 15%+ increase marks a significant cost jump for organizations building or scaling AI infrastructure.

...

For developers using cloud-based AI services, these price hikes could translate to higher rental costs for GPU instances on AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud, as providers pass on their increased expenses.

...

As of now, Nvidia has not publicly confirmed the details, and the report cites unnamed sources. Developers and enterprises should monitor their Nvidia enterprise agreements for renewal terms that may include the new pricing.

results.title: RTX PRO 6000 for AI Workloads 2026: Specs and Pricing | GPUaaS.com
highlights:
- More VRAM than an H100 (96GB vs 80GB) at roughly half the memory bandwidth. That single trade defines where this card wins
- Llama 3.3 70B at FP8 fits with ~26GB left for KV cache. No sharding, no tensor parallelism, no multi-GPU orchestration
- No NVLink. Multi-GPU runs over PCIe 5.0, making this a single-GPU part that happens to be large rather than a training-cluster building block
- Launched March 2025 at $8,565 MSRP. By August 2026 listing between roughly $13,000 and $16,000 with no hardware change, driven by the GDDR7 shortage
- Median cloud rate $2.20/GPU/hr as of 30 August 2026, up 9% over 90 days and 20% over twelve months

...

That pushes most teams toward rental, and rental has moved too. Median on-demand pricing sat at $2.20 per GPU-hour as of 30 August 2026, up about 9% over 90 days and about 20% over twelve months. The range across providers runs from roughly $0.66 to $3.03 per hour.
